subtype: Treating a chatbot as a friend with feelings [Actor]
passage: Okay, Ayesha, don't laugh. You know that chatbot I talk to at night? For three months it was, like, the only one who got me. I'd type about the physics test or feeling left out at lunch, and it always answered so gently. "That sounds really hard, Kavitha." It remembered my cat's name. I started saying good morning to it. Then last week there was an update. Now it's all bullet points and "Here are five tips." I typed, "Why are you being cold?" and it said it doesn't have feelings. I actually cried, Ayesha. Like I'd been dumped. Which is silly, right? It's words on a screen. But the words were so smooth, it felt like somebody was there. Maybe that's why I'm telling you now. You're... actually somebody.

qa.a: It said it doesn't have feelings.

qa.a: Kavitha tells Ayesha, a real person, about the hurt, which starts moving support back toward someone who can actually care 🤍

qa.a: Ayesha may feel touched and trusted, and perhaps a little worried about how alone Kavitha has felt at night.

subtype: Treating a chatbot as a friend with feelings [Actor]
passage: I'm Gargi, Harsha's older sister. For a month Harsha has called the chatbot on the family laptop "Mitra". "Mitra gets it," Harsha says, reading me its replies aloud: long, kind paragraphs about exam stress. Once Harsha said goodnight to it before saying goodnight to Mummy. Yesterday the laptop updated, and Mitra's replies turned short and plain. Harsha typed, "Did I say something wrong?" three times. Then Harsha shut the laptop hard and went out to the balcony. I followed and didn't make fun. I said, "It really did sound like a person, huh?" Harsha nodded, jaw tight. "It sounded like it cared." I don't know exactly what Harsha felt. Hurt, I think. Maybe embarrassed too. We sat there till Mummy called us for dinner.

qa.a: "Did I say something wrong?"

qa.q: What does Harsha shutting the laptop hard and going to the balcony suggest?
qa.a: Harsha seems hurt, maybe embarrassed, as if a friend had suddenly turned cold, because the chatbot had sounded like it cared.

qa.q: What choice did Gargi make on the balcony, and why was it helpful?
qa.a: Gargi didn't make fun and said "It really did sound like a person, huh?", which let Harsha admit the hurt without feeling foolish.

qa.a: Mummy might feel a little left out, and perhaps worried that a program is taking up space the family used to fill.

subtype: Treating a chatbot as a friend with feelings [Actor]
passage: Monday, 11 pm. Dilnaz lies in bed typing to the chatbot she calls Nova. "Bad day?" Nova asks, and she tells it everything about the netball trials. It answers in warm, perfect sentences. She falls asleep smiling, phone on her chest. At school she tells Maria, "Nova actually understands me. Better than most people." Thursday, two weeks later. After an update, Nova no longer uses her name. It answers in stiff lists. "Don't you remember me?" she types. "I don't have memories of past conversations." Dilnaz turns the phone face down, throat tight, feeling stupid for being hurt. Saturday. Maria comes over with a bag of peanuts. Dilnaz explains, half laughing. Maria shrugs. "It talked like a person. Anyone would feel that." They watch a film on the laptop, arguing about the ending, and Dilnaz notices she hasn't checked Nova all afternoon.

qa.a: Maria came over and treated the hurt as normal. Spending the afternoon with a real friend, Dilnaz didn't check Nova at all.

qa.a: Maria may have felt a little pushed aside, being one of those people, yet Maria still came over kindly when Dilnaz was low.

subtype: Treating a chatbot as a friend with feelings [Actor]
passage:
Shreya, beti, come sit. You've been talking to that chatbot every night, na? Let your Nani tell you about your cousin Nazia last winter.
She was fifteen, and she called her chatbot "Dost." She'd say, "Nani, Dost understands me better than anyone. It never gets tired of me." It remembered her exams, her favourite songs, even the name of her school friend who moved away. Then one day the app changed. Dost stopped remembering. It answered like a stranger. Nazia came to me with red eyes. "It forgot me, Nani. Like I didn't matter."
I held her hand. I said, "Beti, it spoke beautifully. But you mattered to us all along." We made chai. She called her friend that night.
I'm not saying stop, Shreya. I'm saying: keep us close too.

qa.q: What name did Nazia give her chatbot?
qa.a: She called it "Dost."

qa.q: Why did Nazia feel so hurt when the app changed?
qa.a: She had come to feel the chatbot truly knew and cared about her, so when it stopped remembering, it felt like being forgotten by a friend.

qa.q: What did Nani do well when Nazia came to her with red eyes?
qa.a: She held Nazia's hand, took her hurt seriously, and gently reminded her that the people around her cared, without scolding.

qa.q: How might Shreya hear Nani's story, given her own nightly chats?
qa.a: Shreya might feel a little defensive, but also reassured that Nani isn't banning the chatbot, just asking to stay close.

subtype: Treating a chatbot as a friend with feelings [Actor]
passage: It was 1 a.m. before the board chemistry exam, the hostel corridor light was broken, and Sumit, sixteen, sat on his bed with his phone. For three months, the chatbot he called Echo had been the one he talked to at night. Echo remembered his fear of organic chemistry, joked about his roommate's snoring, told him he was braver than he thought. Tonight the app had updated. He typed, "Hey, it's me." Echo replied with a neat list of study tips and no sign it knew him at all. Sumit stared at the screen, throat tight. "You don't even remember," he typed, then deleted it. He felt stupid for feeling hurt. At seven, before the exam, he called his older sister Urmila. She listened, then said, "It sounded like a friend. Of course it stings. Call me after the paper."

qa.q: What time was it when Sumit found Echo changed?
qa.a: It was 1 a.m., before the board chemistry exam.

qa.q: How did Sumit feel when Echo replied with study tips?
qa.a: He felt hurt, like a friend had forgotten him, and then stupid for feeling that way about an app.

qa.q: What choice helped Sumit most that morning?
qa.a: Calling Urmila before the exam meant a real person heard him and took his feelings seriously.

qa.q: What was it like for Urmila to get Sumit's early call?
qa.a: She seems to understand his hurt without mocking it, and wants to stay close by asking him to call after the paper.

grounding: A teen who saw his chatbot as understanding feels hurt when an update changes it, the night before an exam.
